 ## Search results
Recent work supports aligning textual semantics with behavioral supervision, but provides limited direct evidence for a lightweight, randomly initialized text encoder inside GRU4Rec. [TedRec (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18166) identifies differences between text and ID representations that make simple embedding addition less effective. [ADRec (2025)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0950705125003375) uses supervised and self-supervised contrastive objectives to improve sequence–target semantic alignment. These motivate interaction-conditioned text learning; neither establishes that text similarity alone captures compatibility or immediate purchase intent.

Many prominent approaches violate the no-pretrained-weights constraint: [CALRec (2024)](https://research.google/pubs/calrec-contrastive-alignment-of-generative-llms-for-sequential-recommendation/) relies on PaLM-2, while [SICSRec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.10556) uses LLM-driven modality alignment and a Transformer sequence architecture. Their reported benefits cannot be assumed to transfer to a small GRU trained from scratch.

A constraint-compatible hypothesis, rather than an established result: jointly train a small token embedding plus masked-mean pooling/MLP encoder on supplied titles and descriptions, integrate its features with item-ID embeddings inside one GRU recommender, and add a weak item-ID/text alignment or token-reconstruction auxiliary loss. Keep next-item prediction dominant so shared vocabulary does not force behaviorally different items together. Preserve one checkpoint per category; compare against the corrected GRU baseline using the fixed macro validation HR@10. Sparse-history gains remain an empirical question.

---

The closest direct GRU precedent is [MTAM (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.08598): temporal gates modify information filtering and recurrent state transitions, with a time-aware GRU capturing short-term intent alongside historical memory. More recent work supports adaptive temporal modeling: [CussCtpm (IJCAI 2024)](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/0255) combines GRUs and neural ODEs to represent continuously evolving POI preferences; [SAPM (2025)](https://cis.temple.edu/~jiewu/research/publications/Publication_files/2025-TWeb-Stability-aware%20Preference%20Modeling%20for%20Sequential%20Recommendation.pdf) uses multi-head GRUs and stability-conditioned fusion of long- and short-term interests. [Long-Term Interest Clock (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.15817) retrieves relevant older behaviors and applies time-gap-aware attention, suggesting that temporal relevance need not decrease uniformly with age. These are architectural precedents, not evidence of gains under the pinned Amazon evaluation.

A compatible experimental hypothesis is one jointly trained GRU whose reset/update gates receive normalized log inter-event gaps, optionally with learned per-dimension retention rates so durable interests can survive longer than transient intent. This is a proposed adaptation, not an established result from the cited studies. First verify padding invariance: identical valid histories with different amounts of left padding should produce identical states and scores; padding must neither update hidden state nor advance elapsed time, and readout must select the final nonpadding position. Only then compare ordinary GRU, fixed decay, and learned retention using the same histories, seeds, training budget, and macro validation HR@10. Existing confounded context-removal measurements cannot establish that older history is harmful. Use observed historical timestamps only; do not assume the next interaction time is available at inference.

---

GRU4Rec’s original [top-k loss paper](https://hidasi.eu/assets/pdf/gru4rec_v2_cikm18.pdf) directly addresses easy-negative saturation: ordinary BPR dilutes gradients across negatives, whereas BPR-max emphasizes high-scoring negatives through softmax weights and adds negative-score regularization. BPR-max already performs implicit hard-negative weighting; explicit mining must demonstrate additional benefit. [Sampled-softmax research (2024)](https://zlstwebsite.github.io/Zlst/publication/on-the-effectiveness-of-sampled-softmax-loss-for-item-recommendation/) identifies informative hard-negative gradients and ranking benefits, but also warns that cosine scoring can impair representation-magnitude learning.
